pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Fossils & Palaeontologists (ages 5–7): a fossil is the remains or trace of a living thing preserved in rock, and a palaeontologist is a scientist who studies fossils to learn about dinosaurs and other ancient life.
• Standards — UK (DfE): no KS1 fossil-specific statutory content, but forward-anchors to Y3 'Rocks' (recognise that fossils are found within rock and that they are the remains of living things from long ago); supports KS1 'working scientifically' (observing, identifying) and links to jobs/people who study the world.
• Standards — US (NGSS): builds toward grade-3 3-LS4-1 (use fossil evidence to describe organisms and environments of long ago); at K–2 this is foundational vocabulary/observation.
• Operational details — Secure three recognitions: (1) WHAT a fossil is — remains/traces of a once-living thing, turned to rock; (2) EXAMPLES — bones, teeth, and footprints preserved in rock (seed body vs trace without naming the jargon); (3) WHO — a palaeontologist finds and studies fossils to work out what dinosaurs were like. Keep it observational and concrete: fossils are things you can look at and identify; the scientist is a detective of the past. Clarify a fossil is not the actual living animal and usually not 'dinosaur bones you could eat' but rock in the shape of the original.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5): points to a fossil and says it comes from a living thing long ago. Tier B (~6): says a palaeontologist is a scientist who studies fossils, and names one example (bone/tooth/footprint). Tier C (~7): explains fossils are preserved in rock and are how we learn what dinosaurs were like.
bestPractices: Teach through identification: show real fossil photos (bone, tooth, footprint in rock) and have children spot and name them — recognition before mechanism.
Frame the palaeontologist as a 'detective of the past' who reads clues in rock, giving purpose to the fossils.
Distinguish a fossil (rock in the shape of/replacing the remains) from the living animal and from an ordinary bone — 'turned to stone over a very long time'.
Seed body-vs-trace gently (a bone IS part of the animal; a footprint is a MARK it left) without introducing the technical terms yet.
Connect to real museums/collections so 'fossil' is a concrete thing children may have seen, not an abstraction.
keyRepresentations: A tappable dig-site or museum scene with a fossil bone, a tooth, and a footprint in rock to identify.
Side-by-side: a living animal → its fossil, showing the same shape preserved in stone.
A palaeontologist character with hand tools (brush, chisel) shown at work.
Simple 'fossil or not a fossil?' picture set (fossil bone vs a toy vs a fresh leaf).
commonMisconceptions: 'A fossil is the actual bone/animal, unchanged' — fossils are usually the original replaced by or turned to rock over a very long time.
'Only dinosaurs make fossils' — many living things (shells, plants, fish, footprints) become fossils.
'Palaeontologists study rocks in general / dig up dinosaurs that are still whole' — they study fossils and usually find scattered, incomplete remains.
'Fossils are found just lying around loose' — they are preserved IN rock and must be carefully found and freed.
'A footprint isn't a fossil because it isn't a body part' — preserved footprints (traces) are fossils too.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: a fossil is the preserved remains or trace of a once-living thing, usually preserved in rock (often turned to stone) over a very long time; a palaeontologist is a scientist who finds and studies fossils to learn about dinosaurs and other ancient life. The target is recognition — say what a fossil is, identify examples (bone, tooth, footprint in rock), and name the scientist's job — plus two conceptual guards: a fossil is not the actual unchanged animal, and a trace like a footprint counts as a fossil too.

activities.title: Dig-site and museum: tap the clues
feedback: On the bone: 'a bone turned to rock — part of a real animal from long ago'.
On the tooth and footprint: name each and say what it tells us (a bone/tooth is part of the animal; a footprint is a mark the animal left).
On the palaeontologist: 'a scientist who finds and studies fossils to learn about dinosaurs', calling out the brush and chisel they use.

If a child thinks the fossil is the actual foot or bone that simply went hard: a footprint was never the foot — the animal pressed its foot into soft mud and walked on, and over a very long time the mud holding the print hardened into rock that keeps its shape. A fossil bone is different: over a very long time, minerals from water soaked into the buried bone and filled or replaced it, so it became stone in the bone's shape.
activities.rationale: The whole target is observational recognition, so a single rich scene where children spot and name real fossil types (bone, tooth, footprint in rock) teaches directly, and anchoring the scientist as the person reading these clues gives the fossils a purpose. Showing where a fossil ends up (museum case) keeps 'fossil' concrete rather than abstract.
sourceClaims: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of once-living organisms, preserved in rock; the original material is typically replaced by minerals over long periods.
A palaeontologist is a scientist who studies fossils to understand ancient life; UK Y3 'Rocks' introduces that fossils are found within rock and are remains of living things from long ago.
learnerActions: Explore an illustrated dig-site and museum scene with several things to find and name.
Tap a knobbly shape half-buried in rock and read the caption: 'a bone, turned to stone, from a real animal that lived long ago'.
Tap a pointy tooth and a footprint pressed into rock; each reveals what it is and what it tells us about the animal.
Tap the person kneeling with a small brush and chisel to learn: 'a palaeontologist — a scientist who finds and studies fossils to figure out what dinosaurs were like'.
Follow a drill-down zoom that carries a fossil from the ground into a museum case, so you see where these clues end up.
Say in your own words what a fossil is and what a palaeontologist does.
activities.intendedInsight: Fossils are real clues preserved in rock (bones, teeth, and footprints all count), and there is a job that is all about finding and reading them.

activities.title: Fossil or not a fossil?
feedback: Fossil bone: yes — a once-living thing preserved in rock.
Toy dinosaur: not a fossil — it was never alive; it is made of plastic.
Fresh leaf: not a fossil yet — it is alive/recent and has not been preserved in rock over a long time (though plants and leaves can become fossils).
If a child brings up footprints and doubts they count: footprints are traces, and preserved traces are fossils too.
activities.rationale: A quick contrast check locks in the recognition and gently separates 'fossil' from an ordinary object or a present-day thing, surfacing the common idea that only certain things count.
sourceClaims: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of once-living organisms, preserved in rock; the original material is typically replaced by minerals over long periods.
learnerActions: Look at a short picture set: a fossil bone in rock, a plastic toy dinosaur, and a fresh leaf.
For each, decide 'fossil' or 'not a fossil' and say why.
Lift a flap to check the answer and read a short reason.
activities.intendedInsight: A fossil is a preserved remains or trace of something that was once alive, kept in rock over a very long time (often turned to stone) — not a toy and not a fresh, present-day thing.

activities.title: Brush away the rock: uncover and sort a dig (optional motivating vehicle)
feedback: Name each find as it is sorted and note 'a palaeontologist does exactly this'.
Reinforce that fossils are usually preserved in rock and often must be carefully freed, so palaeontologists work slowly and gently.
activities.rationale: A brush-and-sort dig maps directly onto the palaeontologist's job and is highly engaging, but the concept is recognition — so this is a motivating vehicle rather than necessary for the understanding. A sort can check that a child classifies finds correctly, though it does not by itself elicit an explanation; the dragging and brushing make the 'finding and freeing' idea concrete.
sourceClaims: A palaeontologist is a scientist who studies fossils to understand ancient life; UK Y3 'Rocks' introduces that fossils are found within rock and are remains of living things from long ago.
learnerActions: Brush or scrape away virtual rock to reveal a hidden fossil.
Drag each find — a bone, a tooth, a footprint — to a labelled tray.
Read the name of each find as you sort it.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding, freeing and sorting fossils is part of what a palaeontologist does — fossils are often carefully freed from rock rather than simply picked up.

activities.title: Footprint puzzle: is it a fossil, and whose foot is it? (check of understanding)
feedback: Full: footprints count (they are traces), the stony print is not the foot itself but the mark it left in mud that hardened into rock, keeping the print's shape; scientists who study fossils are palaeontologists.
If a child says only bones are fossils: broaden the definition — footprints, dung and burrows are fossils too, because they are preserved evidence of a living thing.

If a child says the stone is the real foot that went hard: the foot was never in the stone — the dinosaur pressed it into soft mud and walked on, and over a very long time the mud holding the print hardened into rock that keeps the print's shape (an impression).

If a child says fossils are just rocks that look like animals or things people carved: connect fossils back to real creatures that lived and died; compare a fossil bone to a modern bone of the same shape.
activities.rationale: Two linked questions discriminate between distinct misconceptions: whether a trace counts, and whether the fossil is the actual unchanged body. Only a child who understands a fossil as a preserved remains-or-trace, with the original replaced or moulded, answers both parts.
sourceClaims: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of once-living organisms, preserved in rock; the original material is typically replaced by minerals over long periods.
learnerActions: Consider: someone finds a dinosaur footprint turned to stone. Is that a fossil, even though it isn't a bone?
Then decide: is the stony footprint the dinosaur's actual foot that got hard, or is it something else? Explain.

Try the follow-ups: if the dinosaur's foot isn't in the stone, how can the stone still show its shape? Name two other things besides a footprint that could become a fossil. What do we call a scientist who studies fossils?
activities.intendedInsight: A fossil is any remains OR trace of a long-ago living thing preserved in rock, so footprints count; the stony footprint is not the foot itself — the dinosaur pressed its foot into soft mud and walked on, and over a very long time the mud holding the print hardened into rock, keeping the shape.

constraints: Keep it observational and concrete at ages 5–7: fossils are things you can look at and identify; the scientist is a 'detective of the past'.
Distinguish a fossil (rock in the shape of/replacing the remains) from the living animal and from an ordinary fresh bone — 'turned to stone over a very long time'.
Seed body-vs-trace gently (a bone is part of the animal; a footprint is a mark it left) without introducing the technical terms 'body fossil' / 'trace fossil' yet.
Address the misconception that only dinosaurs make fossils: shells, plants, fish, and footprints can all become fossils.

Address that fossils are usually found in rock and often must be carefully freed (though some wear out of the rock over time and are found loose on the ground or a beach), and that palaeontologists usually find scattered, incomplete remains rather than whole dinosaurs.

Picture-matching or multiple-choice ('which is a fossil?', 'what is a fossil scientist called?') can check recognition but offers fixed options rather than open discovery, so it may add little new teaching beyond the tappable scene — use it as a quick check rather than the main lesson.

A friendly fossil-hunter character answering 'what is this?' is on-theme; for a simple recognition target a guided tap-to-reveal may be more predictable than open dialogue — if used, keep the character's answers short and concrete.
The brush-and-sort dig is an optional engagement vehicle, not required for the recognition goal.
Tappable hotspots, lift-the-flap checks, drag-to-tray sorting, and zoom drill-downs are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; none is mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources remain marked verified:false and were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source describes replacement of original material by minerals over long periods; for ages 5–7 this is simplified to 'turned to stone / the shape filled in and hardened', and a footprint is described as a mould/impression rather than mineral replacement. These are age-appropriate simplifications of distinct preservation processes (body replacement vs trace impression) and could be refined for an older audience.

A 3D interactive was judged to add navigation overhead without improving recognition; this is a design preference for this recognition target, not evidence that 3D cannot help — do not treat as a universal rule.
Comparisons that one medium (tap-to-reveal, quiz, dialogue) is more or less reliable are design judgements for this target, not tested efficacy findings; they use 'may' wording accordingly.
Claims about where fossils 'end up' (museum case) and the detective framing are pedagogical framings, not source-cited facts.

The NGSS grade-3 (3-LS4-1) forward-anchor and the Tier A/B/C checkpoint ages from the original pedagogy summary were not carried into this guidance; reinstate them if progression-level detail is needed.

probeDeeper: If the real foot is gone, how can the stone still show its shape?
Name two other things, besides a footprint, that could become a fossil.
What do we call a scientist whose job is finding and studying fossils?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes, it's a fossil — a fossil is any remains or trace of a long-ago living thing preserved in rock, so footprints count as well as bones and teeth. It is NOT the actual foot: the real foot is long gone. The dinosaur pressed its foot into soft mud, and over a very long time that print filled in and hardened to rock, keeping the shape. Scientists who study fossils are called palaeontologists.

errorPatterns.pattern: A fossil must be a bone — a footprint doesn't count.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden the definition to traces: footprints, dung and burrows are fossils too, because they are preserved evidence of a living thing.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — only bones are fossils, not footprints.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that the footprint is a fossil.

errorPatterns.pattern: The fossil is the dinosaur's actual body or foot that simply went hard.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain the mould/replacement: the original rots away, and rock takes on its shape over a very long time.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's the real foot that turned hard.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the stone is the real preserved foot, with no idea of replacement or a mould.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fossils are just rocks that happen to look like animals, or things people carved.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect fossils back to real creatures that lived and died; compare a fossil bone to a modern bone of the same shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies fossils come from real once-living organisms.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks only bones are fossils, or that a fossil is the animal's actual unchanged body, or that fossils aren't from real creatures.
responseLevels.full: Defines a fossil as remains OR traces of a once-living thing preserved in rock (footprints included), explains the original is gone but its shape is kept, and names the palaeontologist.
responseLevels.partial: Knows fossils are old remains in rock, but is unsure a trace like a footprint counts, or can't say the original has been replaced or moulded.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone finds a dinosaur footprint turned to stone. Is that a fossil, even though it isn't a bone? And is the stony footprint the dinosaur's actual foot that got hard, or is it something else? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks only bones are fossils denies the footprint; a child who thinks a fossil is the animal's own preserved body says the foot went hard. Only a child who understands a fossil as a preserved remains-or-trace, with the original replaced or moulded, answers both parts — which the tier-two 'actual foot or something else' pins down.
